alignment.note: The Vulgate transmits an entirely different verse (Mark 9:43 on cutting off the hand), not the Greek/Peshitta warning about causing little ones to stumble (Mark 9:42). This represents a major textual divergence, likely a versification or manuscript tradition error in the input data.

Greek σκανδαλίσῃ ('cause to stumble') and Peshitta ܕܢܟܫܠ (d-nakhshel, 'cause to stumble') align semantically, but Vulgate scandalizaverit applies to a different subject ('if your hand causes you to stumble'), confirming the verse mismatch.

Greek ἕνα τῶν μικρῶν τούτων ('one of these little ones') and Peshitta ܠܚܕ ܡܢ ܗܠܝܢ ܙܥܘܪܐ (l-ḥad men hālen z'ūrē, 'one of these little ones') align precisely. Vulgate te manus tua ('your hand') refers to a completely different object, confirming the verse is Mark 9:43, not 9:42.

Greek τῶν πιστευόντων εἰς ἐμέ ('who believe in Me') and Peshitta ܕܡܗܝܡܢܝܢ ܒܝ (d-mhaymnin bi, 'who believe in Me') align with identical participial construction. Vulgate abscide illam ('cut it off') belongs to the hand-cutting pericope, not the stumbling-block warning.

Greek καλόν ἐστιν αὐτῷ μᾶλλον ('better it is for him rather') uses comparative adverb μᾶλλον post-verbally; Peshitta ܦܩܚ ܗܘܐ ܠܗ (pqaḥ hwā leh, 'better it-would-be for-him') employs periphrastic construction with enclitic pronoun; Vulgate bonum est tibi ('good it-is for-you') omits the comparative intensifier but conveys equivalent meaning.

Greek εἰ ('if') introduces the conditional protasis; Peshitta ܐܠܘ (elū, 'if/would that') functions identically. Vulgate debilem introire in vitam ('to enter life maimed') belongs to the hand-cutting verse's apodosis, not the millstone conditional.

Greek περίκειται μύλος ὀνικὸς ('is placed a millstone of-donkey') uses the compound adjective ὀνικός to specify a large donkey-driven mill. Peshitta ܪܡܝܐ ܗܘܬ ܪܚܝܐ ܕܚܡܪܐ (rmyā hwat rḥyā d-ḥmārā, 'were-cast millstone of-donkey') employs passive participle + auxiliary, with ܕܚܡܪܐ as genitive construct. Vulgate duas manus habentem ire ('having two hands to go') continues the hand-cutting verse, not the millstone image.

Greek περὶ τὸν τράχηλον αὐτοῦ ('around the neck of-him') uses prepositional phrase with article; Peshitta ܒܨܘܪܗ (b-ṣawreh, 'on-his-neck') employs preposition ܒ + pronominal suffix, a more compact Syriac idiom. Vulgate in gehennam in ignem inextinguibilem ('into Gehenna, into unquenchable fire') describes the destination of the hand-cutting verse, not the millstone's placement.

Greek καὶ βέβληται εἰς τὴν θάλασσαν ('and he-has-been-cast into the sea') uses perfect passive indicative with prepositional phrase. Peshitta ܘܫܕܐ ܒܝܡܐ (w-shdē b-yamā, 'and-cast in-the-sea') employs active participle coordinated with preceding passive, typical Syriac parataxis. Vulgate omits this clause entirely, as the verse transmitted is Mark 9:43, which ends with the Gehenna reference.
